title: Kepler-90i: a deep convolutional neural network finds an eighth planet in archival Kepler data
summary: A Google/UT Austin neural network found Kepler-90i in archival Kepler data; NASA announced it on 14 December 2017 and the AJ published it on 30 January 2018.
account: On 14 December 2017 NASA announced a deep convolutional neural network had identified an eighth planet, Kepler-90i, in archival Kepler Space Telescope data. Christopher Shallue (Google Brain) and Andrew Vanderburg (University of Texas at Austin, NASA Sagan Fellow) built it. It was trained on about 15,000 previously vetted Kepler signals and correctly identified true planets and false positives 96 percent of the time in testing. It was then applied to 670 known multi-planet systems to search for weak transit signals missed by earlier methods. Kepler-90i is a rocky planet about 30 percent larger than Earth with a 14.4-day orbit. It was statistically validated together with Kepler-80g, an Earth-sized sixth planet in a resonant chain. The peer-reviewed paper appeared in the Astronomical Journal on 30 January 2018.
purpose: Built to classify Kepler transit signals as planets or false positives and to recover planets missed by earlier searches. This benefit was that purpose.
system: Deep convolutional neural network for Kepler transit-signal classification (Shallue and Vanderburg)
developer: Google (Christopher Shallue, Google Brain) with Andrew Vanderburg (University of Texas at Austin)
deployer: Shallue and Vanderburg, applied to NASA Kepler archival data

ratings.reason: NASA's Paul Hertz said that discoveries were lurking in archived Kepler data awaiting the right tool. The archive yielded two newly validated planets without new telescope observations by the authors. Their validation used Kepler data and follow-up observations that other observers had already uploaded to the Kepler Community Follow-up Program.

Astronomy gained a validated eighth planet and the first exoplanetary system known to have eight planets, tying the Solar System. This is a knowledge gain for a specialist community rather than a population-level benefit.

ai_role.statement: The neural network ranked the weak Kepler-90i transit signal above false positives in systems that earlier automated and human searches had already examined. The authors then statistically validated both new planets. The AI did the identification. Validation used conventional methods.

comparator.quote: Automated tests, and sometimes human eyes, are used to verify the most promising signals in the data. However, the weakest signals often are missed using these methods. Shallue and Vanderburg thought there could be more interesting exoplanet discoveries faintly lurking in the data.

later.note: The same group adapted the network as AstroNet-K2 for the K2 mission and used it to identify and validate two previously unknown exoplanets.
later.quote: We train a convolutional neural network, called AstroNet-K2, to predict whether a given possible exoplanet signal is really caused by an exoplanet or a false positive. AstroNet-K2 is highly successful at classifying exoplanets and false positives, with accuracy of 98% on our test set.

fields.account: On 14 December 2017 NASA announced a deep convolutional neural network had identified an eighth planet, Kepler-90i, in archival Kepler Space Telescope data. Christopher Shallue (Google Brain) and Andrew Vanderburg (University of Texas at Austin, NASA Sagan Fellow) built it. It was trained on about 15,000 previously vetted Kepler signals and correctly identified true planets and false positives 96 percent of the time in testing. It was then applied to 670 known multi-planet systems to search for weak transit signals missed by earlier methods. Kepler-90i is a rocky planet about 30 percent larger than Earth with a 14.4-day orbit. It was statistically validated together with Kepler-80g, an Earth-sized sixth planet in a resonant chain. The peer-reviewed paper appeared in the Astronomical Journal on 30 January 2018.
